items.prompt: Match each mixture to the best way to separate it.
hints: Look at what is different about the two materials in each mixture: size, dissolving or magnetism.
Sieves sort by size, filters catch insoluble bits, evaporation leaves dissolved solids and magnets pick up iron.
Start with the iron nails. Think about which method picks up only some metals.
items.explanation: A sieve separates big pieces from small ones, and a filter traps insoluble sand. Evaporating the water leaves the salt behind, and a magnet pulls out the iron.

items.prompt: Ravi has muddy water with sand in it. What should he use to remove the sand?

options.why: Sand is not magnetic, so a magnet cannot pick it up.

options.text: a filter paper in a funnel

options.why: Grains of sand are tiny and would pass through large holes.
A thermometer measures temperature. It cannot separate anything.

hints: Sand does not dissolve in water. It is an insoluble solid.
You need something with holes small enough to stop sand grains but let water through.
Cross out the tools that measure or attract things.
items.explanation: Filter paper has tiny holes that let water through but trap the grains of sand. This method is called filtering.

items.prompt: A mixture contains sand and iron filings. Which is the quickest way to separate them?

options.why: Neither sand nor iron dissolves, so both would stay on the filter paper together.
There is no water to evaporate, and both solids would be left together.
Sand grains and iron filings are about the same size, so a sieve cannot sort them.

hints: Think about a property that iron has but sand does not.
Some metals are pulled towards a magnet.
Cross out the methods that sort by size or need water.
items.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sand is not. A magnet pulls the iron filings out and leaves the sand behind.

items.prompt: Why can filter paper not separate salt from salty water?

options.text: Dissolved salt is in pieces so tiny that they pass through the filter paper.

options.why: Salt is not magnetic, and magnetism has nothing to do with filtering.

options.text: Filter paper dissolves in salty water.
options.why: Filter paper does not dissolve. It stays whole while water passes through.

options.text: Salt is too big to pass through.
options.why: If the salt were too big, the filter would catch it. Dissolved salt passes through.

hints: When salt dissolves, it breaks into particles too small to see.
A filter only stops pieces that are bigger than its tiny holes.
Compare the size of dissolved salt particles with the holes in filter paper.
items.explanation: When salt dissolves, it splits into particles small enough to pass through the holes in filter paper with the water. To get the salt back, you must evaporate the water.

items.prompt: A mixture contains iron filings, sand and salt. Choose 3 methods that together separate all three.

options.text: dissolving the salt, then filtering out the sand
evaporating the water from the salty liquid

options.why: All three are small grains, so a sieve cannot sort them.
These materials melt only at very high temperatures, and melting would not separate them.

hints: Each of the three materials has a different property you can use.
Iron is magnetic, salt dissolves in water and sand does not dissolve.
Take out the iron first. Then add water to the sand and salt, and think about the next step.
items.explanation: A magnet removes the iron filings. Adding water dissolves the salt, filtering removes the sand, and evaporating the water leaves the salt behind.

items.prompt: Rock salt is salt mixed with sand and grit. Put the steps in order to get clean salt from it.
items: evaporate the water from the salty liquid
hints: Sand and grit do not dissolve, but salt does.
First the salt must dissolve, then the sand can be removed, then the salt can be collected.
Start by making the lumps of rock salt smaller so the salt dissolves faster.
items.explanation: Crushing makes small pieces, and stirring in water dissolves the salt. Filtering removes the sand and grit, and evaporating the water leaves clean salt.

items.prompt: On the island of Madura, farmers let sea water stand in shallow ponds in the dry season. How do they get salt?

options.text: The salt sinks and the water is poured away.
options.why: Dissolved salt does not sink. The water has to evaporate.
Madura is warm, and sea water does not freeze there.

options.text: The Sun's heat evaporates the water and leaves the salt behind.
Filtering the sea water traps the salt.
options.why: Dissolved salt passes through a filter. The water must evaporate instead.

hints: Sea water is a solution of salt in water.
Think about what the hot, dry season does to shallow water.
Ask which part of the sea water can turn into a gas and leave the pond.
items.explanation: The Sun's heat makes the water evaporate, leaving the dissolved salt behind as crystals. Shallow ponds and dry weather help the water evaporate faster.

items.prompt: Which mixture is best separated with a sieve?

options.why: Salt dissolves, so it passes straight through a sieve. Evaporate the water instead.
Both are tiny grains of a similar size. Use a magnet instead.
Sugar dissolves, so it passes through a sieve. Evaporate the water instead.

hints: A sieve separates pieces of different sizes.
Look for a mixture with one big kind of piece and one small kind of piece.
Cross out the mixtures where one part has dissolved.
items.explanation: Pebbles are too big to fit through the holes of a sieve, but sand grains fall through. Dissolved materials pass straight through a sieve with the water.

items.prompt: Draw how to filter muddy water using a funnel, filter paper and a beaker. Label the funnel, filter paper, beaker, sand and clean water.

criteria.label: Draws a funnel sitting in a beaker
Shows filter paper folded inside the funnel
Shows the sand trapped on the filter paper
Shows clear water collected in the beaker

hints: Draw the beaker first, then put the funnel on top of it.
Think about where the sand ends up and where the water ends up.
items.explanation: The filter paper sits inside the funnel above the beaker. Sand is trapped on the paper, and water drips through into the beaker.

items.prompt: Kiki builds a filter from gravel, sand and cloth. Dirty river water comes out looking clear. Is it safe to drink?

options.why: Clear water can still contain microorganisms that are too small to see.

options.text: Yes, because sand kills all germs.
options.why: Sand traps bits of dirt, but it does not kill microorganisms.

options.text: No, because filtering adds salt to the water.
options.why: A filter does not add salt.

options.text: No. Tiny microorganisms can pass through, so the water should be boiled first.

hints: A filter traps pieces that are bigger than the gaps between its grains.
Some microorganisms that cause illness are far too small to see.
Ask whether a sand filter can stop something smaller than the gaps in it.
items.explanation: A sand filter removes mud and bits, but harmful microorganisms are small enough to pass through. Boiling the water kills them, which makes it safe to drink.
